summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets and throughput for chat streaming use case. Nimbus wants sub-300ms p95 for short responses and 15-20 RPS sustained at 50 token responses with spikes to 150 concurrent streams. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private trade-offs, batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization impact and plan to run token/sec benchmarks with Redwood samples.
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sofia, AE at Redwood, and with me is Liam our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Marta (Nimbus): Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to chat.
[00:12] Priya (Nimbus): Hi, thanks for setting this up. We're trying to nail down latency and throughput for a chat feature across web and mobile.
[00:20] Liam (Redwood): Great. Quick agenda: understand your targets (p95), concurrency, typical prompt lengths, and decide whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private fits. Then we can propose a benchmark plan.
[00:30] Evan (Nimbus): Sounds good. To kick off, our primary SLA ask is p95 under 300ms for short system messages (~30-60 tokens). For typical user chat turns ~50 tokens we'd like p95 under 400ms. We also need sustained throughput: baseline 15-20 RPS of 50-token responses with capacity to handle spikes to 150 concurrent streams.
[00:50] Sofia (Redwood): OK that's very helpful. When you say 150 concurrent streams, is that open streaming (server-sent events) per user connection or many requests being opened simultaneously?
[00:58] Priya (Nimbus): Streaming per user, yes — we do progressive tokens to the client. So token/sec and time-to-first-byte matter a lot.
[01:07] Liam (Redwood): For streaming usecases the p95 to first token is often the critical metric. We can optimize that with prefix KV cache and smaller initial decoding steps. The hosted API can hit low latencies for single-shot but at high concurrency you might want Dedicated so we can reserve GPUs and shape autoscaling.
[01:27] Marta (Nimbus): Can you give rough numbers — like tokens/sec or ms per token — so we can map to our cost model?
[01:33] Liam (Redwood): Sure. Roughly speaking, on a modern A100-style instance a 7B-ish model quantized can do ~1.5-3k tokens/sec single-stream with batching disabled, but latency to first token may be 120-250ms depending on sequence length and model. For Transformer decoder heavy models, when you enable continuous batching throughput increases a lot — aggregated tokens/sec goes up, but per-stream p95 can rise if you wait to batch.
[02:00] Priya (Nimbus): So batching hurts p95 but helps cost — we trade latency vs cost.
[02:04] Liam (Redwood): Exactly. We expose batching policies. For real-time streaming you'd configure small batch windows and KV caching to keep p95 tight. For high concurrency, Dedicated gives predictable cluster sizing so we don't hit queuing as easily.
[02:18] Evan (Nimbus): What about model variants? We use a tuned 6B model in prod. If we quantize to 4-bit do we save latency or cost?
[02:25] Liam (Redwood): Quantization mainly reduces memory and can improve throughput (more simultaneous sessions per GPU). But 4-bit quant can sometimes slightly increase per-token latency if certain kernels aren't optimal, though usually overall tokens/sec increases. We recommend benchmarking your actual model and prompt mix.
[02:42] Sofia (Redwood): Also worth noting our smart routing: you can route lower criticality traffic to hosted spot or cheaper profiles and keep critical traffic on Dedicated. That helps with cost while meeting p95 for priority users.
[02:54] Priya (Nimbus): We're also concerned about tail spikes during flash sales — our concurrency distribution has heavy tails. How do you handle sudden 3-5x bursts?
[03:04] Liam (Redwood): Two levers: burst capacity (Dedicated can have burst pools) and graceful degradation — automatic fallback to a smaller model variant or lower token limit for non-critical flows. Additionally, autoscaling and queueing policies with SLA-aware prioritization are available.
[03:20] Marta (Nimbus): How about private deployment? We have compliance concerns for some customer segments.
[03:25] Sofia (Redwood): Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you control over network egress and KMS. Performance is similar but you manage infra; Redwood provides the control plane and optimizations. For strict data residency or SOC 2+ requirements, many customers choose Private.
[03:40] Evan (Nimbus): So for our immediate needs — low p95 and spikes — you'd recommend Dedicated to start?
[03:44] Liam (Redwood): Yes for the spike profile and predictability. Hosted may work for a while, but Dedicated reduces queuing variance for p95.
[03:50] Priya (Nimbus): Let's talk benchmarking. What do you need from us to run meaningful token/sec and p95 tests?
[03:56] Liam (Redwood): Representative prompt set (preferably 100-200 prompts), distribution of response lengths, desired concurrency shape (RPS, percentiles), and a sample of streaming vs single-shot breakdown. We'll run mixed workloads: 50-token average, 150-token bursts, and a heavy short-turn traffic to capture first-token p95.
[04:17] Sofia (Redwood): We'll share a benchmark template. Our SE team will run both hosted and Dedicated staging runs, report p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, time-to-first-byte, and GPU util.
[04:27] Priya (Nimbus): Great — what duration should tests be? We saw some vendors use short runs that don't capture warming/kv cache benefits.
[04:34] Liam (Redwood): We usually do warmup + sustained 15-30 minute steady-state runs and a long tail spike test for 5-10 minutes. Warming matters for prefix cache and kernel JIT.
[04:46] Marta (Nimbus): Any gotchas re streaming that we should measure differently?
[04:50] Liam (Redwood): Measure first-byte p95 and end-to-end Jitter. Also measure tokens/sec per client and aggregate. For streaming, network RTT and chunking size affect perceived latency. We'll instrument and give you per-route traces.
[05:03] Evan (Nimbus): Security questions: we need SSO, SAML, RBAC, and audit logs. Also KMS integration for Private.
[05:11] Sofia (Redwood): We support SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and audit logs. Private supports customer KMS/HSM. We'll attach SOC 2 and architecture docs.
[05:21] Priya (Nimbus): Pricing — how do you price Dedicated? Flat reserved capacity? And bursting cost?
[05:27] Sofia (Redwood): Dedicated is reserved GPU pools with monthly/annual commits. Burst capacity is an add-on or negotiated in the contract. Hosted is usage-based. We'll send a pricing sheet with examples mapped to your target RPS and token/sec.
[05:39] Priya (Nimbus): For our cost model we need per-1k-token cost at baseline and under heavy batching.
[05:44] Liam (Redwood): We'll include token-level cost and provide examples with different batching windows and quantization profiles.
[05:51] Marta (Nimbus): Can Redwood do canary rollouts and A/B model testing for quality regressions? We need to test quality vs speed tradeoffs.
[05:58] Sofia (Redwood): Yes, rollouts and A/B are built-in — you can route percentages to different model versions and we provide eval hooks and regression alerts tied to prompt eval sets.
[06:08] Priya (Nimbus): Good. One more technical — what's your approach to KV/prefix caching for chat contexts?
[06:13] Liam (Redwood): We support automatic prefix KV caching and reuse across sessions when you pin embeddings or prompt prefixes. That reduces compute for repeated system/template context. It's particularly effective when many users share identical system messages.
[06:27] Evan (Nimbus): Let's try to quantify. If we have a 200-token context with a 50-token reply, what's the typical saving?
[06:33] Liam (Redwood): If prefix is cacheable, you avoid re-encoding the 200-token prefix each request — so you pay only for the 50 tokens in decoding plus KV lookup overhead. In practice that can cut compute by 60-70% for those flows.
[06:45] Marta (Nimbus): OK that's promising. Any constraints on concurrency per GPU?
[06:49] Liam (Redwood): It's model and quantization dependent, but on Dedicated you can plan for X concurrent streaming sessions per A100-style GPU for your model size. We'll provide concrete numbers after we benchmark your model.
[06:59] Priya (Nimbus): Timeline: we'd like to run benchmarks next week if possible.
[07:03] Sofia (Redwood): We'll aim to start baseline runs week of 2026-03-30. I'll send the template today.
[07:09] Evan (Nimbus): Perfect. One last thing — fallbacks: if primary model is saturated, can Redwood auto-failover to smaller model?
[07:16] Liam (Redwood): Yes, policy-based fallback to cheaper/fast model variants is supported and can be tuned by route.
[07:23] Priya (Nimbus): Thanks — this was helpful.
[07:26] Sofia (Redwood): Great. Quick recap of next steps and owners?
[07:29] Marta (Nimbus): Yes please.
[07:30] Sofia (Redwood): Action items — Sofia sends pricing and benchmark template by Monday 3/30; Liam will run staging benchmarks when we get prompts and will schedule infra deep-dive; Priya to share prompts and concurrency profile by 3/31. We'll follow up with a demo of streaming fallbacks in first week of April.
[07:51] Priya (Nimbus): Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[07:54] Sofia (Redwood): Thanks all, we'll follow up via email.
[07:56] [call ends]
